result:
At 4:17 in the morning, the city becomes honest. The buses are sleeping in their depots, their windows black and reflective. The convenience store hums like a small spaceship. Somewhere, a person is mopping a floor they will never own. Somewhere else, a person is practicing a speech nobody will hear. Rain has written temporary rivers along the curb, and every streetlamp keeps one golden coin of light in the water. I walk without destination because destinations feel too demanding before sunrise. A cat watches me from beneath a parked car. We understand each other perfectly: neither of us has planned this life very well.

There is an old man in my neighborhood who feeds pigeons from a blue plastic bucket. He calls each bird by a different name, though I suspect he has forgotten which name belongs to which bird. “Margaret,” he says, scattering seeds. “Charles. Little mayor.” The pigeons arrive with their soft gray bureaucracy, blinking and bowing, accepting their appointments. I once asked him why he did it. He looked surprised by the question. “They’re waiting,” he said. It seemed like an answer to more than pigeons. Since then, whenever I feel useless, I remember that waiting is its own kind of hunger, and perhaps somebody is carrying a blue bucket toward me.

The moon is not romantic when viewed from a laundromat. It hangs over the coin-operated machines like a peeled fruit, pale and faintly bruised. Inside, a woman folds tiny shirts with the careful concentration of an astronomer. A man sleeps sitting upright beside Dryer Six, his arms crossed, his head tilted toward the warmth. The machines turn and turn, displaying their little weather systems behind round glass doors. Socks rise and vanish. A red scarf presses itself against the window, then sinks. I think of all the things people try to clean: shirts, sheets, names, memories, the evidence of being touched.

In a drawer in my kitchen, there is a bent spoon I refuse to throw away. It was bent during an argument, though not dramatically. Nobody hurled it. Nobody shouted. Someone simply leaned too hard against the counter, and the spoon was trapped beneath an elbow and a bowl. Still, I remember the conversation whenever I see it. That is the trouble with objects: they are too good at keeping secrets. A cracked mug remembers a goodbye. A coat remembers a winter. A key remembers every door it failed to open. Even dust remembers, settling gently over abandoned plans, making them look almost peaceful.

Sometimes I imagine that every person has a weather report floating above them, visible only to strangers. Mine would say: scattered optimism, increasing clouds by evening, chance of unnecessary nostalgia after midnight. The man crossing the street with a bouquet would be bright but windy. The teenager dragging a suitcase through the station would have severe pressure changes, possible thunder. The cashier who asks how you are and waits for the real answer would be clear, cool, with remarkable visibility. We would all dress differently if we knew. We would carry umbrellas for one another. We would stop saying, “You seem fine,” when the forecast clearly warned of storms.

A friend once told me that trees communicate through their roots. They send nutrients, warnings, perhaps even something resembling comfort. A sick tree can be supported by the others around it. This fact has ruined loneliness for me. Not cured it—ruined it. Now I cannot sit beneath a grove without suspecting that the silence is crowded with messages. Beneath the dirt, beneath the old bottles and worms and buried coins, there may be a language of need and response. I like to think the forest is always asking, Are you still there? and answering, Yes. Take what you need. Stay a little longer.

There are places that exist only because somebody forgot to remove them. A narrow staircase behind a restaurant. A bench facing a brick wall. A room above a closed bookstore where dust gathers in the shape of former furniture. I love these accidental countries. They ask nothing. They have no admission fees, no gift shops, no official story. You can stand in them and feel briefly unobserved by history. Every famous place has been polished into a sentence. The overlooked places remain unfinished paragraphs, full of doors nobody has bothered to name. Perhaps that is why they feel so generous. They let you bring your own meaning.

I worry that the future will be too bright. Not hopeful—bright. Screens everywhere, windows that darken themselves, streets lit at noon, advertisements blinking in the corners of sleep. I want darkness to survive as a public service. I want children to know the dangerous comfort of a field at night, the way stars become visible only after the world stops insisting on itself. Darkness is not emptiness. It is a room where imagination can sit down. It is a blanket thrown over the machinery. It is permission to admit that we do not know what comes next, and maybe never did.

One day, I will forget the faces of people who mattered to me. Not completely, perhaps. I will remember the outline: a certain laugh, a wristwatch, the habit of pausing before difficult words. But details will leave first. The exact color of their eyes. The shape of their handwriting. The sound their footsteps made in a hallway. This frightens me, until I remember that forgetting is not always betrayal. A river does not dishonor the mountain by moving away from it. The water carries traces. It changes shape. It becomes cloud, rain, tea in a stranger’s cup. Love may work like that: transformed, not erased.

For now, morning arrives without asking permission. Windows brighten one by one. A truck groans down the avenue. The cat beneath the parked car has gone somewhere important. In the convenience store, the cashier flips the sign from CLOSED to OPEN, though it feels as if the world has only changed its costume. I buy coffee that tastes faintly of cardboard and courage. Outside, the rain has stopped. The streets are full of small mirrors, each holding a piece of sky. I step around them carefully, as though I might disturb something. As though the day has been waiting, quietly, for me to begin.
